questions.stem: What observation shows a hydrocarbon is unsaturated in the bromine water test?

options.explanation: The double bond consumes the bromine by addition.
No reaction deepens the reagent's colour.
Nothing precipitates in this test.
The addition consumes both reagents into one product.

questions.stem: Which reaction type consumes bromine water with an alkene?

options.explanation: No acid-base pair operates here.
Both bromine atoms join the molecule at the C=C.
Substitution is the alkane's slow UV reaction.
That is the manganate(VII) chemistry.

questions.stem: Hexane and hexene are shaken separately with bromine water in the dark. What happens?

options.explanation: Hexene's pi bond attacks the bromine readily.
The outcome is exactly reversed.

options.text: Hexane keeps the orange colour; hexene decolourises it
options.explanation: Saturated hexane cannot open the Br-Br bond without UV help.
Hexane is saturated - it leaves the colour alone in the dark.

questions.stem: Why must the alkane comparison be performed in the dark?

options.explanation: Evaporation does not decolourise the reagent.
Alkenes react with bromine water without light.
The reagent is stable without light; the caveat targets the alkane side.

options.text: Sunlight enables slow radical substitution of alkanes with bromine, faking a positive
options.explanation: UV light initiates the radical route that bleaches bromine.

questions.stem: What organic product forms when ethene reacts with bromine water?

options.explanation: One bromine lands on each alkene carbon.
That is the HBr addition product - the second bromine must appear.
Bromine brings no oxygen.
That is the manganate oxidation product.

questions.stem: State the reagent and the observation used to test for a C=C double bond.
questions.modelAnswer: Shake the sample with orange bromine water; decolourisation shows an unsaturated C=C bond is present.

questions.stem: Explain, in one sentence each, why the bromine colour disappears with an alkene but not with an alkane in the dark.
questions.modelAnswer: The alkene's pi bond opens the Br-Br bond and takes both atoms in by addition; the saturated alkane offers no reactive site, so the reagent survives unchanged.

questions.stem: Explain why bromine water is described as testing saturation rather than testing alkenes specifically.
questions.modelAnswer: Any unsaturated hydrocarbon - alkene or cycloalkene - consumes the reagent, while any saturated one survives it, so the test distinguishes the saturation classes rather than one named family.

questions.stem: A colourless liquid X decolourises bromine water in the dark within seconds. State what bond X must contain and name the reaction type you witnessed.
questions.modelAnswer: X must hold a carbon-carbon double bond, and the colour loss was an addition reaction that consumed the bromine across that bond.
